literal: When Qi received the Mandate, his rank was reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: When Northern Qi took the throne, his title was lowered per precedent.

literal: Tan’s younger brother Chang, at the start of his career, was made Regular Attendant of Direct Communication and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Duke of Langye with an open state, fief of five hundred households.
idiomatic: Tan’s brother Chang began as regular attendant of direct communication and cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, Duke of Langye with five hundred household fief.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Zhuang’s reign he was specially enfeoffed Prince of Taiyuan.
idiomatic: At Zhuangdi’s accession he was specially made Prince of Taiyuan.

literal: He was repeatedly promoted to Grand Master of Splendid Happiness; he was promoted out of turn to Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry with the Three Precedents of Protocol.
idiomatic: He rose to grand master of splendid happiness, then was jumped to grand general of chariots and cavalry with protocol of the third rank.

literal: In the second year of Tianping he died; he was posthumously made Duke of Grand Commandant.
idiomatic: He died in Tianping year 2 and was posthumously titled grand commandant.

literal: His son Shanhu inherited.
idiomatic: His son Shanhu succeeded.

literal: When Qi received the Mandate, his rank was reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: When Northern Qi took the throne, his title was lowered per precedent.

literal: Prince of Zhao commandery Gan, styled Sizhi.
idiomatic: Gan, Prince of Zhao commandery, styled Sizhi.

literal: In the ninth year of Taihe he was enfeoffed Prince of Henan, made Grand General of the Guard,[4] and appointed Palace Attendant and Grand Director of the Inner Capital.
idiomatic: In Taihe year 9 he was made Prince of Henan and grand general of the guard,[4] palace attendant, and grand director of the inner capital.

literal: Soon he was given General of Chariots and Cavalry and Grand Master of Brilliant Virtue, and held concurrent office as Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
idiomatic: Soon he was general of chariots and cavalry and grand master of brilliant virtue, with concurrent charge of the Ministry of Personnel.

literal: His birth mother died.
idiomatic: His birth mother died.

literal: Gaozu’s edict said: “Consort Dowager Lady Han has passed away; my feelings are wounded with grief.
idiomatic: Gaozu wrote: "Consort Dowager Lady Han is dead, and grief wounds me.

literal: In the former dynasty’s time the consort dowager’s position matched the Nine Concubines; she shared rank with the highest clans and bore me a brother of the same womb.
idiomatic: In the former reign she had stood among the nine concubines, ranked with the highest houses, and bore my full brother.

literal: Thinking of this orphaned child, I am only moved to compassion; tomorrow I shall go briefly to mourn at the bier—order the outer offices to prepare.”
idiomatic: For this orphaned child I am moved to pity; tomorrow I shall go briefly to mourn—have the outer offices prepare."

literal: He sent a palace attendant with forged credentials to oversee the funeral, and bestowed eight hundred bolts of colored silk.
idiomatic: He sent a palace attendant with forged credentials to oversee the rites and gave eight hundred bolts of colored silk.

literal: An edict said: “In a degenerate age affairs are many, and feeling is wrested by reason.
idiomatic: An edict read: "In a troubled age affairs crowd in, and private feeling must yield to duty.

literal: Gan already holds a weighty post and bears the scales of appointment—how can he indulge his private wish and leave his charge vacant?
idiomatic: Gan already holds a weighty post and bears the scales of appointment—how can he indulge private grief and neglect his charge?

literal: Send a Yellow Gate Gentleman to instruct and urge him to strive in princely affairs with effort; I shall soon meet with him myself.”
idiomatic: Send a Yellow Gate gentleman to urge him back to his duties; I shall see him soon."

literal: He was appointed Bearer of the Staff, Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in the three provinces of South Yu, Ying, and East Jing, Grand General Who Pacifies the South, with an open office, and Inspector of Yu Province.
idiomatic: He was made bearer of the staff, commander-in-chief of South Yu, Ying, and East Jing, grand general who pacifies the south, with open office and inspectorate of Yu.

literal: When the imperial carriage campaigned south, Gan was made Bearer of the Staff, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, and commander of all military affairs west of the Pass; he was given ten bronze tiger tallies, and the classics and histories were separately bestowed.
idiomatic: On the southern campaign Gan was bearer of the staff, grand general of chariots and cavalry, and commander west of the Pass, with ten bronze tiger tallies and a separate gift of the classics.

literal: Gaozu loved his younger brothers deeply; because Gan commanded troops on a separate route, he admonished him: “Minister of Works Mu Liang in years and capacity may be your teacher; Regular Attendant of Direct Communication Lu Yuan’s talent may be consulted—you should take them as masters.”
idiomatic: Gaozu loved his brothers; as Gan took a separate command he warned him: "Mu Liang, minister of works, is fit to be your teacher in years and counsel; Lu Yuan, regular attendant of direct communication, is fit to consult—take them as masters."

literal: Soon, because Xiao Ze died, the army withdrew.
idiomatic: Soon Xiao Ze died and the army withdrew.

literal: After the move to Luoyang he was changed to Prince of Zhao commandery, appointed commander of all military affairs in the three provinces of Ji, Ding, and Ying, Grand General Who Campaigns East, and Inspector of Ji Province; his open office was as before, and five hundred assorted items were bestowed, and again ten catties of gold were secretly given.
idiomatic: After the capital moved to Luoyang he became Prince of Zhao commandery, commander of Ji, Ding, and Ying, grand general who campaigns east, and Ji inspector, his open office unchanged; he received five hundred assorted gifts and ten catties of gold in secret.

literal: Gaozu personally saw him off in the near suburbs and addressed Gan: “The principles of punishment and imprisonment are what the ancient sages found difficult; yet once there is a state, one cannot but urge oneself.
idiomatic: Gaozu saw him off near the capital and told him: "Punishment and imprisonment are what sages found hardest; yet with a realm in your charge you must urge yourself.

literal: You are my fine younger brother—you should continue to cultivate virtue and gloriously exalt Wei; think deeply and plan far, as if treading on thin ice above a deep abyss.
idiomatic: You are my fine brother—cultivate virtue and exalt Wei; think deep and plan far, as on thin ice over an abyss.

literal: If you rely on kinship’s weight and do not attend to the affairs of the age, the state has its constant statutes, and sorrow will only increase.”
idiomatic: If you lean on kinship and neglect public duty, the state has fixed law, and grief will follow."

literal: Gaozu’s edict made Li Ping chief clerk, Tang Mao marshal, and Lu Shangzhi advising officer to correct and assist him.
idiomatic: Gaozu named Li Ping chief clerk, Tang Mao marshal, and Lu Shangzhi advising officer to guide him.

literal: Yet when Ping and the others remonstrated, Gan utterly would not accept it.
idiomatic: When they remonstrated, Gan would not heed them.

literal: The province memorialized the beheading of a horse-thief; by statute the penalty was excessive, yet the Masters of Writing, because Gan had just taken office, indulged him and did not impeach.
idiomatic: The province reported a horse-thief beheaded; the penalty exceeded statute, but the Masters of Writing, since Gan had just arrived, indulged him and did not impeach.

literal: An edict said: “Punishment is to restrain people; guilt must not be excessive—thus when punishments miss the mark the people have nowhere to set foot.
idiomatic: An edict said: "Punishment restrains the people; guilt must not run wild—when punishments miss the mark the people have nowhere to stand.

literal: If killing by awe alone were truly good, then it should be applied broadly through all the provinces.
idiomatic: If terror alone were virtue, every province should do the same.

literal: If restriction is needed, how can one fail to measure against the correct canon?
idiomatic: If restraint is needed, why not measure against the canon?

literal: Moreover the statutes and ordinances have no provision for a new lord to add executions;
idiomatic: Statutes nowhere allow a new lord extra executions;

literal: the ritual canon and old regulations do not record the beauty of exclusive authority at first arrival.
idiomatic: ritual canon nowhere praises exclusive severity on first taking office.

literal: The Masters of Writing bent to my private intent and truly wounded imperial magnanimity.
idiomatic: The Masters of Writing bent to my whim and truly wounded imperial magnanimity.

literal: Gan is dark in governance and imposed heavy punishments outside the law—both may be investigated and reported.”
idiomatic: Gan is blind in rule and imposed extra-legal severity—investigate and report both."

literal: Later he was transferred to Special Grand Mentor and Governor of Si Province.
idiomatic: He was later made special grand mentor and governor of Si.

literal: When the imperial carriage campaigned south, an edict made Gan commander of all military affairs within and without, gave one set of martial music, three hundred armored men, and permission to pass through the palace gates.
idiomatic: On the southern campaign Gan was made commander of all armies within and without, given martial music, three hundred armored guards, and passage through the palace gates.

literal: Gan was greedy and licentious and did not follow the statutes; the Inspector of the Masters of Writing Li Biao was about to impeach him.
idiomatic: Gan was greedy and licentious and scorned law; Inspector Li Biao was about to impeach him.

literal: He happened to meet Gan in the Masters of Writing’s lower lodging, and so, screening those beside them, said to Gan: “Your Highness, of late there have been reports, and I am about to raise an impeachment; I fear it will harm the sage’s trust in you—if you reform past conduct and cultivate what is to come, Biao will say nothing; if you do not repent and reform, tonight’s word will be tomorrow’s memorial.”
idiomatic: He met Gan in the Masters of Writing quarters, dismissed attendants, and said: "Highness, reports have reached me and I mean to impeach you—yet that would wound the emperor's trust. Reform, and I stay silent; fail to repent, and tonight's warning becomes tomorrow's memorial."

literal: Yet Gan was at ease and took no notice; Biao thereupon memorialized an impeachment.
idiomatic: Gan took no notice; Biao memorialized the impeachment.

literal: When Gaozu read it he was angry and grieved; he ordered Gan and Prince of Beihai Xiang to follow the crown prince to the traveling palace.
idiomatic: Gaozu read it in anger and ordered Gan and Prince of Beihai Xiang to follow the crown prince to the traveling palace.

literal: When they arrived, Xiang alone was granted audience; Gan was not received.
idiomatic: At arrival Xiang alone was received; Gan was not admitted.

literal: He secretly ordered those beside him to observe Gan’s expression and color; knowing there was no worry or repentance, he personally enumerated his faults, beat him one hundred strokes, removed him from office, and sent him back to his residence as prince only.
idiomatic: He had attendants watch Gan's face; seeing no remorse, he counted his faults in person, beat him a hundred strokes, stripped his offices, and sent him home as prince only.

literal: In the twenty-third year he died, aged thirty-one.
idiomatic: He died in year 23, aged thirty-one.

literal: Eastern Garden secret vessels and fifteen suits of burial garments were given; three thousand bolts of condolence silk; posthumous title Prince Ling; he was buried with honor at Changling.
idiomatic: He received Eastern Garden rites, fifteen burial suits, three thousand bolts of condolence silk, posthumous name Prince Ling, and burial at Changling.

literal: His son Mi, at the beginning of Emperor Shizong’s reign, inherited the enfeoffment.
idiomatic: His son Mi inherited at Shizong's accession.

literal: Gan’s consort Lady Mu memorialized that Mi’s mother Zhao and others were contrary to ritual and constantly at fault, increasingly insubordinate day by day; the distinction of honor and baseness was blocked, and the way of mother and son was severed.
idiomatic: Consort Lady Mu reported that Mi's mother Zhao and others broke ritual daily, blocked honor and baseness, and severed mother and son.

literal: An edict said: “A concubine toward her lady is like a daughter-in-law toward parents-in-law; the rites between ruler and subject admit no doubling of meaning.
idiomatic: An edict read: "A concubine to her lady is as a daughter-in-law to parents-in-law; ruler and subject admit no double standard.

literal: A concubine’s son toward his lord-mother—the rites add the son’s reverence; how can they profane my customs and government!
idiomatic: A concubine's son owes his lord-mother a son's reverence—how dare they profane my customs?"

literal: Hand them over to the Director of the Imperial Clan and punish according to ritual.”
idiomatic: Hand them to the Director of the Imperial Clan for ritual punishment."

literal: During mourning for his mother Mi listened to music and drank and played; he was impeached by Inspector of the Masters of Writing Li Ping.
idiomatic: In mourning for his mother Mi listened to music and drank; Inspector Li Ping impeached him.

literal: He encountered an amnesty and was restored to his enfeoffment.
idiomatic: An amnesty restored his title.

literal: He was appointed Regular Attendant of Direct Communication, made Dragon-Charger General, transferred to Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent, and sent out as Champion General and Inspector of Qi Province.
idiomatic: He was regular attendant of direct communication, dragon-charger general, junior tutor of the heir, then champion general and Qi inspector.

literal: Mi’s nature was severe; he was violent and cruel toward subordinates.
idiomatic: Mi was severe and brutal to those below him.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Suzong’s reign an imperial envoy Yuan Yan reached his provincial border.
idiomatic: Early in Suzong's reign the imperial envoy Yuan Yan reached his border.

literal: Because relay posts and patrols had no troops, he took command to inspect and verify.
idiomatic: Finding relay posts without troops, he took command to inspect.

literal: Squad chief Gao Baoyuan listed in detail all troops held— the prince had impressed them all for private service.
idiomatic: Squad chief Gao Baoyuan listed every soldier—the prince had impressed them all for private use.

literal: When Mi heard it he was greatly enraged and flogged Baoyuan and four others two hundred strokes each.
idiomatic: Mi flew into a rage and flogged Baoyuan and four others two hundred strokes each.

literal: Within a few days Mi summoned corvée labor from nearby provinces, closed the city’s four gates, made inner and outer defenses strict, searched the city, and plundered to the utmost.
idiomatic: Within days he summoned corvée from nearby provinces, sealed the four gates, tightened inner and outer defense, and searched the city with plunder to the utmost.

literal: Again, without cause, he beheaded six men.
idiomatic: Without cause he beheaded six more.

literal: The whole city was fierce with fear; the crowd thereupon shouted at the garrison gates.
idiomatic: The whole city shook with fear; the crowd shouted at the garrison gates.

literal: Mi was afraid; he went up a tower and destroyed the stairs to hold himself secure.
idiomatic: Terrified, Mi climbed a tower and destroyed the stairs to hold himself secure.

literal: The local people scattered and fled; the townspeople divided to guard the four gates.
idiomatic: Locals fled; townspeople split to hold the four gates.

literal: Empress Dowager Ling sent Mobile-Column General Wang Jing by urgent relay to instruct him.
idiomatic: Empress Dowager Ling sent mobile-column general Wang Jing by urgent relay to instruct him.

literal: When the townspeople saw Jing had arrived they opened the gates to beg pardon and handed over the seals of office.
idiomatic: When the town saw Jing they opened the gates in surrender and handed over the seals.

literal: Mi was thereupon removed from his province.
idiomatic: Mi was removed from the province.

literal: On his return he was appointed Grand Minister of Agriculture.
idiomatic: On return he was grand minister of agriculture.

literal: He was again appointed Regular Attendant of the Palace Secretariat, Pacifier of the North General, and Inspector of You Province.
idiomatic: He was again regular attendant of the palace secretariat, pacifier of the north, and You inspector.

literal: Mi’s consort Lady Hu was a cousin on Empress Dowager Ling’s side.
idiomatic: Consort Lady Hu was Empress Dowager Ling's cousin.

literal: Before he set out, for beating his consort he was removed from office.
idiomatic: Before he departed he was stripped of office for beating his consort.

literal: Later he was appointed Director of the Ministry of Justice and made Pacifier of the South General.
idiomatic: Later he was director of the ministry of justice and pacifier of the south.

literal: In the fourth year of Zhenguang he died.
idiomatic: He died in Zhenguang year 4.

literal: Eastern Garden secret vessels, one set of court dress, and one suit of garments were given; five hundred bolts of condolence silk.
idiomatic: He received Eastern Garden rites, one court dress, one suit of garments, and five hundred bolts of condolence silk.

literal: Prince of Gaoyang Yong, Gan’s younger brother by the same mother, memorialized arguing for Mi; therefore he was posthumously promoted in excess to Acting Palace Attendant, General Who Pacifies the South, and Governor of Si Province; posthumous title Zhenjing.
idiomatic: Yong, Prince of Gaoyang and Gan's uterine brother, pleaded for Mi; Mi was posthumously raised to acting palace attendant, general who pacifies the south, and Si governor, titled Prince Zhenjing.

literal: His son Yu, styled Zichun, inherited.
idiomatic: His son Yu, styled Zichun, succeeded.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Zhuang’s reign he met disaster at Heyin; he was posthumously made Grand General of the Guard with the Three Precedents of Protocol and Inspector of Qing Province; posthumous title Xuangong.
idiomatic: At Zhuangdi's accession he died at Heyin and was posthumously grand general of the guard with protocol of the third rank and Qing inspector, titled Prince Xuangong.

literal: He had no son; an edict made Mi’s younger brother Chen’s son Zhen, styled Jingrong, his heir, and he inherited the rank.
idiomatic: Childless, an edict made Chen's son Zhen, styled Jingrong, his heir; he inherited the title.

literal: When Zhen’s elder brother Chen was again enfeoffed Prince of Zhao commandery, he was changed to Prince of Pingchang.
idiomatic: When Zhen's elder brother Chen was restored as Prince of Zhao commandery, Zhen was changed to Prince of Pingchang.

literal: When Qi received the Mandate, his rank was reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: When Northern Qi took the throne, his title was lowered per precedent.

literal: His son Wei inherited.
idiomatic: His son Wei succeeded.

literal: When Qi received the Mandate, his rank was reduced by precedent.
idiomatic: When Northern Qi took the throne, his title was lowered per precedent.

literal: Mi’s younger brother Tan was quite forceful in standing; in youth he was esteemed and respected among the imperial clan.
idiomatic: Mi's younger brother Tan was forceful by nature and esteemed in the clan from youth.

literal: From Supervisor of the Feathered Forest he went out as Administrator of Gaoyang; his government was severe and decisive, and the powerful feared him.
idiomatic: From feathered-forest supervisor he went out as Gaoyang administrator; his rule was severe and the powerful feared him.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Suzong’s reign he entered service as Direct-Gate General, passed through Grand Master of the Stud and Junior Director of the Imperial Clan, and was made Champion General.
idiomatic: At Suzong's accession he became direct-gate general, then grand master of the stud and junior director of the imperial clan, and champion general.

literal: When Yuan Faseng rebelled abroad, an edict made Tan Bearer of the Staff, Acting Left General, and detached commander to campaign against him.
idiomatic: When Yuan Faseng rebelled, Tan was made bearer of the staff, acting left general, and detached commander against him.

literal: When Xuzhou was pacified he was transferred to Junior Master of Brilliant Happiness, acting Administrator of South Yan Province, General Who Subdues the Barbarians, and Inspector of Jing Province.
idiomatic: After Xuzhou was pacified he was junior master of brilliant happiness, acting south Yan administrator, general who subdues the barbarians, and Jing inspector.

literal: He entered service as Martial Guard General.
idiomatic: He entered as martial guard general.

literal: Soon an edict made Tan commander to campaign against Du Luozhou; he halted at Jundu and was defeated by Luozhou.
idiomatic: Soon he was made commander against Du Luozhou, halted at Jundu, and was beaten.

literal: On his return he was appointed Pacifier of the West General and Inspector of Qin Province.
idiomatic: On return he was pacifier of the west and Qin inspector.

literal: He died; he was posthumously made General Who Pacifies the Army with the Three Precedents of Protocol and Inspector of Qing Province.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously general who pacifies the army with protocol of the third rank and Qing inspector.

literal: The text is deficient.
idiomatic: The text is deficient.

literal: Chen’s younger brother Xian was by nature greedy and violent without propriety; from Supervisor of the Feathered Forest he was transferred to Chief Clerk of the Ministry of State.
idiomatic: Chen's brother Xian was greedy, violent, and without propriety; from feathered-forest supervisor he rose to chief clerk of the ministry of state.

literal: In Emperor Suzong’s time he was appointed Regular Gentleman; he was gradually promoted to Left General and Grand Master of the Palace.
idiomatic: Under Suzong he was regular gentleman, then left general and grand master of the palace;

literal: He was enfeoffed Baron of Pingxiang with an open state, fief of two hundred households.
idiomatic: he was baron of Pingxiang with two hundred household fief.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Zhuang’s reign he met disaster at Heyin.
idiomatic: At Zhuangdi's accession he died at Heyin.

literal: He was posthumously made Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry with the Three Precedents of Protocol and Inspector of Ding Province.
idiomatic: He was posthumously grand general of chariots and cavalry with protocol of the third rank and Ding inspector.

literal: His son Jingxuan was Direct-Gate General.
idiomatic: His son Jingxuan was direct-gate general.

literal: He followed the Deposed Emperor and was lost west of the Pass.
idiomatic: He followed the Deposed Emperor and was lost west of the Pass.

literal: Xian’s younger brother Xu was Supervisor of the Feathered Forest and Direct-Gate General.
idiomatic: Xian's brother Xu was feathered-forest supervisor and direct-gate general.
